newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia wharf workers strike over IR bill.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia wharf workers strike over IR bill.

text.p: Australian waterfront workers walked off the job in all major ports on Tuesday to protest the Senate passing secondary boycott provisions in a new Industrial Relations Bill earlier in the day, the Maritime Union of Australia (MUA) said.
MUA joint national secretary John Coombs said the move to prevent the MUA and other unions from taking solidarity action was a threat to democracy and the Australian way of life.
"This is draconian legislation," he said in a statement. "It outlaws solidarity."
The legislation took away the right of workers to strike, Coombs said.
Exact figures were not immediately available on the number of vessel which would be affected but about 60 are normally in Australian ports at the same time.
Of those, only about 10 vessels, mostly in iron ore and other bulk commodity export ports around Australia, would not be hit because of non-union workers.
"It's a pretty unsatisfactory situation," said John Jenkins, executive director of the Chamber of Shipping.
"They certainly will not resolve matters (by calling a strike). It will strengthen resolve that the government's industrial relations legislation is needed," he said.

The conservative Liberal-National coalition government elected in March introduced a bill to replace the industrial relations legislation of the former Labor government that the coalition said gave too much power to unions.

However, to enable the new laws to pass the upper house, where the coalition does not have a majority, the government had to reach a compromise on many clauses with the minority, left-leaning Australian Democrats.
The secondary boycott provisions, that severely curb the right to strike by workers not directly involved in a dispute, passed the Senate on Tuesday afternoon.
The rest of the act is now before the Senate.
Australian dockworkers have a long history of taking industrial action for political purposes, which would be caught up by the new legislation.
